\section[la herida]{la herida — the wound, the injury}

\label{lesson:ES-C525-herida}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for the alarm, then the Spanish for to evacuate.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: la herida}
\textbf{la herida} — \textquotedblleft{}the wound, the injury\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Tiene una herida en la pierna.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{He has a wound on his leg.}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{herida} is built on the participle of \emph{herir} 'to wound', which is inherited from Latin \emph{ferīre} 'to strike' (EtymDB).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{la herida}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{la herida}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{la herida}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for the alarm, then the Spanish for to evacuate, then say \emph{la herida} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does la herida mean? (\textquotedblleft{}The wound, the injury\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[herir]{herir — to wound, to injure; to hurt}

\label{lesson:ES-C525-herir}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for to evacuate, then the Spanish for the wound.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: herir}
\textbf{herir} — \textquotedblleft{}to wound, to injure; to hurt\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
El accidente hirió a dos personas.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The accident injured two people.}
\end{quote}

Stem change: \emph{hiero}, \emph{hirió}. It also hurts feelings: \emph{Me hirió lo que dijo.}

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{herir} is inherited from Latin \emph{ferīre} 'to strike', through old Spanish \emph{ferir} (EtymDB). Latin \emph{f-} became Spanish \emph{h-}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{herir}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{herir}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{herir}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for to evacuate, then the Spanish for the wound, then say \emph{herir} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does herir mean? (\textquotedblleft{}To wound, to injure; to hurt\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la ambulancia]{la ambulancia — the ambulance}

\label{lesson:ES-C525-ambulancia}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for the wound, then the Spanish for to wound.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: la ambulancia}
\textbf{la ambulancia} — \textquotedblleft{}the ambulance\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
La ambulancia llegó en cinco minutos.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The ambulance arrived in five minutes.}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{ambulancia} was borrowed from French \emph{ambulance}, a word usually explained as first naming a field hospital that moved with an army. It is built on Latin \emph{ambulāre} 'to walk' (Lewis \& Short).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{la ambulancia}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{la ambulancia}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{la ambulancia}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for the wound, then the Spanish for to wound, then say \emph{la ambulancia} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]

\section[socorrer]{socorrer — to help, to come to the aid of}

\label{lesson:ES-C525-socorrer}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for to wound, then the Spanish for the ambulance.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: socorrer}
\textbf{socorrer} — \textquotedblleft{}to help, to come to the aid of\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Unos vecinos socorrieron a los heridos.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{Some neighbours came to the aid of the injured.}
\end{quote}

\emph{¡Socorro!} — help! \emph{Socorrer a alguien} — to help someone in danger.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{socorrer} is inherited from Latin \emph{succurrere} 'to run up, to run to help' (EtymDB), built on \emph{sub} and \emph{currere} 'to run' (Lewis \& Short).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for to wound, then the Spanish for the ambulance, then say \emph{socorrer} again

\section[el herido]{el herido — the injured person; injured}

\label{lesson:ES-C525-herido}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for the ambulance, then the Spanish for to help.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: el herido}
\textbf{el herido} — \textquotedblleft{}the injured person; injured\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Hay tres heridos graves.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{There are three people seriously injured.}
\end{quote}

As an adjective: \emph{Está herido} — he is injured.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{herido} is built on the participle of \emph{herir} 'to wound', which is inherited from Latin \emph{ferīre} 'to strike' (EtymDB).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}
